A model receives numerical representations of an instruction, an image, or a joint angle.
To understand its inputs, separate the original quantity, the operation that represents it, and the objective used to learn from it.
An ID, an embedding vector, and a physical coordinate have different roles even when a model processes them in one sequence.

## Four transformations with different jobs {#four-transformations-with-different-jobs}

| Transformation | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| [Quantile normalization](../robotics/quantile-normalization.qmd) | Physical coordinate | Scaled continuous number |
| [Text tokenization](representations.qmd#sentencepiece) | String | Discrete vocabulary IDs |
| [Embedding lookup](representations.qmd#embeddings) | Vocabulary ID | Learned vector |
| [Visual encoding](representations.qmd#visual-tokens) | Image patches | Continuous feature vectors |

An ID identifies an entry in a finite vocabulary; an embedding is a vector used in computation.
A sequence position can therefore hold an embedding without having a corresponding vocabulary ID.
[PaliGemma, §3.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07726), illustrates this distinction: text passes through a tokenizer and embedding lookup, while visual features pass through a learned projection.

## Text pieces, IDs, and embeddings {#sentencepiece}

SentencePiece is a tokenisation framework supporting algorithms including BPE and unigram models.
Calling a tokenizer “SentencePiece” does not identify its segmentation algorithm, vocabulary, or preprocessing rules.
A BPE model uses learned merge rules for frequent adjacent symbols; a unigram model scores candidate segmentations using a learned vocabulary model.
The loaded model file determines the behaviour.
The [official SentencePiece documentation](https://github.com/google/sentencepiece) describes these alternatives and the distinction between pieces and IDs.

## IDs and Embedding Vectors {#embeddings}

For a text string, tokenisation produces IDs $z_1,\ldots,z_n$.
An embedding matrix $E\in\mathbb R^{V\times d}$ contains one learned row for each of $V$ vocabulary entries:

$$
  e_i=E[z_i,:]\in\mathbb R^d.
$$

The ID is an index, so subtracting two IDs does not measure semantic distance.
The embedding has learned coordinates, which are subsequently modified by the Transformer.
Tokenisation and contextual representation learning are distinct stages.

## State Bins Serialized as Text {#state-bins}

In [OpenPI's PaliGemma tokenizer](https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi/blob/main/src/openpi/models/tokenizer.py), the $\pi_{0.5}$ path bins normalised state coordinates, serialises the resulting integers as text, and tokenises that string together with the instruction.
Thus a state coordinate, its bin number, and the text IDs spelling that number are three different objects.
One coordinate need not correspond to one text token.
The observed implementation assumes an appropriate normalised range and does not explicitly clip before binning; values below its lowest edge can receive index $-1$.
“256 bins” therefore does not, by itself, establish out-of-range handling.

## Image tokens are continuous features {#visual-tokens}

A vision Transformer projects patches of image pixels into vectors, adds positional information, and lets these vectors exchange information through attention.
Its final patch features need not describe only their original patches because attention introduces wider context.

PaliGemma uses the image encoder from SigLIP and projects its output vectors to Gemma's embedding width.
It concatenates those vectors with embedded text tokens.
There is no step that assigns each image patch a text-vocabulary ID in this path, and PaliGemma does not use SigLIP's original text tower as its language model.
These are architectural statements from [PaliGemma, §3.1 and Figure 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.07726).

The word *token* describes a sequence element here.
It does not imply discrete quantisation, next-token prediction, or one named object per element.

## Follow the Learning Objective {#follow-the-learning-objective}

[Contrastive image–text learning](representation-learning.qmd#clip-and-siglip) explains CLIP and SigLIP's paired-image-and-text objectives.
Its [pretraining discussion](representation-learning.qmd#representation-pretraining-and-policy-training) separates the origin of an encoder's weights from the objective used by a downstream policy.
[Activation normalization](normalization.qmd#what-to-check-when-reading-a-model) transforms internal activations and has a different role from scaling physical input or output coordinates.

## Paper Connections {#paper-connections}

[PaliGemma](../../literature-review/multimodality/paligemma.qmd) combines projected visual vectors with embedded text.
[FAST](../../literature-review/action/fast.qmd) converts continuous action trajectories into discrete targets.
[π0.5](../../literature-review/action/pi05.qmd) shows why a physical state coordinate, its quantized bin, and the text IDs representing that bin must be distinguished.

## Connections {#connections}

[Quantile normalization](../robotics/quantile-normalization.qmd) develops continuous coordinate scaling and its inverse.
[Attention](attention.qmd#projections) updates representations using permitted positions; [activation normalization](normalization.qmd#what-to-check-when-reading-a-model) transforms their internal statistics.
[Representation learning](representation-learning.qmd) explains training and adapting the encoders that produce these vectors.
[Cross-entropy](../mathematics/entropy.qmd#cross-entropy) evaluates predicted distributions over discrete targets.
The [ViT review](../../literature-review/vision/vit.qmd) gives the patch projection and transformer architecture.
[FAST](../../literature-review/action/fast.qmd) tokenizes temporal action trajectories, while [PaliGemma](../../literature-review/multimodality/paligemma.qmd) and [π0](../../literature-review/action/pi0.qmd) use visual features to condition other outputs.
